title: contextual-drift-field-notes
body:
Purpose and quick summary:

- Quick brain dump about "contextual drift": the tendency for an LLM's behavior/outputs to slowly change across long sessions or repeated interactions, even when the prompt stays semantically the same. Trying to surface practical failure modes for production chat flows and outline lightweight evals to measure drift.

High-level notes / intuition:

- Observed phenomena in prod-ish experiments: subtle style shifts (e.g., more verbose over time), hallucination rate creeping up in long-context RAG sessions, and sometimes token-level repetition that compounds.
- Potential causes: KV-cache aliasing or reduced precision in long KV chains; internal attention saturating on recent tokens; prompt/temperature interaction over repeated calls; stochasticity compounding when sampling without strong anchors.
- Distinguish between transient state (recoverable with an explicit anchor prompt) vs permanent drift (model output distribution changes unless reset). Important for UX because users think app is flaky.

Papers / reads pulled together (quick takeaways):

- Paper A: "Temporal Consistency in Dialogue Models" (recent workshop). Key point: adding short anchor prompts every N turns drastically reduces persona drift. Experiments on 2B–20B models, consistent across sampling strategies.
- Blog post: "When the model forgets the goal" — emphasizes scalar supervision (reward shaping) mitigates drift but is heavy-handed.
- Kernel note: quantization + KV compression can introduce non-linear effects on long contexts; some microbenchmarks show a sharp bump in perplexity at certain context lengths (possible catastrophic rounding).

Concrete examples from my sandbox (notes-to-self):

- Session A (RAG chat, 16k window, 8-bit quantized variant): after ~9k context tokens, answer brevity reduced, started injecting small factual errors about entity dates. Resetting the conversation fixed it instantly.
- Session B (stateful assistant with memory): repeated clarifying questions made the assistant adopt a more tentative tone and started hedging with "I might be wrong" after the 12th turn — users noticed trust drop.

Evaluation designs to try (prioritized):

1) Drift rate curve (cheap):
   - Metric: KL-distance or embedding-drift between the model's answer distribution at turn t vs turn 0 for identical question anchors interleaved across sessions.
   - Setup: sample 200 anchor prompts; run sessions of length 20/50/100 turns; record answers at anchored positions.
   - Notes: need deterministic sampling (top-k deterministic) vs standard sampling to separate sampling noise from drift.

2) Anchor resilience test:
   - Insert canonical anchor prompts (firm instructions + small example) every N turns to see how often they restore original behavior.
   - Sweep N in {5,10,20}.

3) KV-cache corruption probe:
   - Run synthetic sequences that generate near-duplicate key vectors (e.g., repeating long phrases with minor edits) to test eviction/collision impacts.
   - Metric: per-token loss and downstream answer correctness.

4) Quantization cliff test:
   - Vary quantization modes (16/8/4-bit variants) and measure where drift/bump appears in context length.

Experiment logistics / infra notes:

- Prefer running on Dedicated dev pool to get consistent timings and identical kernels. Need 3 model variants: unquantized fp16, 8-bit LLM-adapted, and experimental 4-bit.
- Use deterministic seeds for baseline runs; capture KV-cache internal checksums (if possible) and timestamps for first/last occurrence of drift.
- Capture streaming logs and token-level latencies — drift sometimes correlates with slow tail latencies which cue the runtime to change batching behavior.

Immediate small test I can run (this week):

- Implement the Drift rate curve with 50 anchors and session length 40 against the 8-bit and fp16 variants. Use a mix of factual questions, style anchors (e.g., "Respond in 3 words"), and logic puzzles. Quick metric = fraction of anchors that differ semantically (embedding similarity threshold).

Design questions / unresolved hypotheses:

- Is drift primarily an inference-runtime artifact (KV collision, precision) or model-internal (attention dynamics)? Likely both — need orthogonal tests.
- Do prompts with stronger safety anchors (e.g., repeated system messages) degrade performance due to over-conditioning? Tradeoffs to quantify.
- How much of observed drift is user-facing vs invisible (only measurably different by embedding metrics but not affecting UX)?

Operational mitigations to consider (if drift confirmed):

- Periodic soft anchors: silently inject a tiny instruction every N tokens (opt-in per product).
- Session reset heuristics: reset cache after X tokens or when drift metric exceeds threshold. Must evaluate cost/latency UX tradeoff.
- Enhanced KV encoding: explore alternate hashing/position-keying to reduce aliasing.
- Monitoring: add drift alarms in Console (per-session drift score + rolling baseline) and surface to engineers via SLI.

Notes-to-self / TODOs:

- [ ] Finalize anchor prompt set (50 canonical anchors across styles).
- [ ] Implement small harness to run anchors across model variants (approx 2k calls, cost estimate ~ $60 on dev pool).
- [ ] Chat with SRE (Mika) about capturing KV checksums or enabling extra logging in dev Dedicated cluster.
- [ ] File an issue linking early logs to see if any kernel selection changes around drift windows.

References / links I want to read next:

- A couple of kernel/quantization posts from midsummer 2029 about "lowbit cliff effects" (save urls here).
- Papers on dialogue consistency and long-range attention stability (collect more).

Quick user impact note for product folks:

- If drift is real and common across our standard stacks, it could explain rising support tickets about "assistant getting weird after long chats" and justify offering "session-stability" as a paid feature (e.g., persistent anchors + monitoring).

Closing: this is preliminary. Want to run the simple anchor/embedding test this sprint and report back with a small dashboard (drift vs session length) and a short write-up for product.
